The ONNX pack: weights to Q4NX, matmuls to our kernels, no VitisAI#

Design note for deliverable 4. It answers one question: if a model arrives as a plain ONNX graph, what does it take to run it on this NPU without executing a single AMD custom operator?

What a "Ryzen AI pack" is, and why we do not execute one#

The AMD Ryzen AI toolchain ships prebuilt ONNX packs: a graph whose transformer blocks are replaced by nodes in a custom domain (com.amd.*), each one executed by a compiled xclbin through the VitisAI execution provider, with weights pre-quantised into that provider's own layout. It is fast and it is opaque: the pack decides the quantisation, the kernel, the tiling and the schedule, and the operator that runs on the device is a black box the vendor compiles.

We do not execute those operators. Three concrete reasons, in the order they bind:

  1. Licence and footprint. The VitisAI EP arrives in the AMD wheel, which the contract forbids us from linking or shipping. A pack that only runs through com.amd.* nodes therefore cannot run in our binary at all.
  2. We already own the kernels. npu/ generates and launches the int8 × int8 GEMM that the forward route uses (ONEBIT_NPU lane), with our own quantisation, our own tiling and a layout we can debug with xrt::elf tooling. A vendor pack would replace a measured component with an unmeasured one.
  3. The graph must stay a graph. Our plugin EP's value is that ONNX Runtime schedules the graph and our provider takes the matmuls it has a kernel for; everything else stays on the CPU EP. A pack with fused custom nodes removes exactly that composability.

So the pack we design is the same idea, built from parts we control: ONNX graph stays plain, weights become Q4NX on disk, each matmul shape is bound to a kernel we generated, and the EP is the thing that does the binding at run time.

What the graph gives us#

Census of qwen3-0.6b.onnx (from onnx/export_qwen3.py --check, opset 21, ai.onnx domain only, float32, seq dynamic):

MatMul (K, N) count projection kernel today
1024 × 151936 1 lm_head none — CPU EP
1024 × 3072 56 gate, up none — CPU EP
3072 × 1024 28 down none — CPU EP
1024 × 2048 28 q full_i8_QKV_K1024_N2048_m16.elf
2048 × 1024 28 o none — CPU EP
1024 × 1024 56 k, v full_i8_O_K1024_N1024_m16.elf

254 MatMul nodes, 6 distinct shapes, zero custom domains. The binding is therefore a table lookup on (K, N), which is exactly what ONEBIT_EP_NPU_ELFS="16x1024x2048=<elf>,16x1024x1024=<elf>" already expresses; a shape with no entry returns ORT_NOT_IMPLEMENTED, the EP falls back to the CPU for it, and the session still runs. That is why deliverable 4 can be honest about owning 84 of 254 matmuls rather than claiming the model.

The three layers of the pack#

1. Weights: Q4NX on disk, int8 + scales in the kernel's layout. The on-disk format is already Q4NX-family (4-bit blocks with per-block scales, the format npu/q4nx.cpp decodes). At session start we bind a weight tensor by pointer identity and call the runtime's own packB, which quantises each column to int8 with scale = amax/127 and stores the column scales alongside the packed buffer — the same function the forward route calls, so the numerics of a packed weight cannot drift from the weights the forward route would have used. Packing happens once per (tensor, K, N); the EP caches one slot per bound kernel and repacks when the pointer changes.

2. Activations: per-row int8 with amax/127. Every matmul input is quantised per row, on the device's own scale convention, and the dequant multiplies back C = Cm * ascale[row] * wscale[col]. This is the forward route's exact arithmetic; the measured device error on a 1024 × 1024 matmul is max_abs 9.893e-02 of max|ref| 20.414 (rel 4.846e-03) against a 2 % gate, so the int8 path is inside the tolerance the proof asserts.

3. Shapes: one ELF per (M, K, N), generated not fetched. An ELF is compiled for a fixed tiling (_m16 here, 16 rows per launch). The pack step is therefore a coverage problem, not a compatibility problem: for every (K, N) in the census we either have a generated ELF or we do not, and the plan is to generate the missing ones with the existing generator rather than to reshape the model.

shape owner today next step
q 1024×2048, k/v 1024×1024 our EP done, proven on the device
o 2048×1024, down 3072×1024 CPU EP generate m16 ELFs, same generator
gate/up 1024×3072 CPU EP same
lm_head 1024×151936 CPU EP needs a vocab-blocked kernel (N far past one ELF); leave on the CPU until the FFN set is proven

What the pack does not do, deliberately#

  • No KV cache. The exported graph re-runs the whole sequence per step, so its tokens/s is that graph's rate and is never compared against a KV-cached server. A cached graph is a different, much larger piece of work; pretending otherwise would put a misleading number in the release notes.
  • No fp16, no int4 activations. The kernel is int8 × int8 → int32; the 4-bit-ness of the checkpoint lives on disk and is a memory-bandwidth story, not a compute one. An int4 tensor-core kernel would need a different ELF, and nothing here blocks that later.
  • No vendor operators, ever. If a shape has no kernel it goes to the CPU EP. That keeps the failure mode boring: a slower session, never a session that refuses to load because a custom domain is missing.

Where the numbers live#

The device measurements (tokens/s with our EP on q/k/v vs the CPU-EP control, and KL(forward‖ort) against 1bit npu-run) belong in ~/briefs/TORTEP-STATE.md under deliverable 4, with the exact commands. This note is the design; the state file is the evidence.

A8W8 QDQ, the shape Quark emits#

AMD's Quark ONNX-to-ONNX flow (the 2025 Ryzen AI NPU quantisation article; Linux-only) writes a QDQ graph rather than a custom-op graph: every tensor that used to be float becomes

x_q  --DequantizeLinear(s_x, zp_x)-->  x_dq  \
                                              MatMul --> y  --QuantizeLinear(s_y, zp_y)--> y_q
w_q  --DequantizeLinear(s_w, zp_w)-->  w_dq  /

with int8 activations and int8 weights (A8W8), float32 scales, and the same pattern at A16W8, Xint8 (power-of-two scales), BF16/BFP16, MX4/6/9, MXFP4/MXINT8 and Int4 weight-only, using GPTQ, AdaRound, AdaQuant, SmoothQuant or QuaRot to pick the scales. That is the good news: A8W8 is exactly what our device kernel already computes — int8 × int8 into int32, dequantised by one scale per activation row and one per weight column.

Why it folds without a new kernel#

Our GEMM is C_s32[m][n] = Σ_k a_q[m][k]·w_q[k][n], dequantised as C = C_s32 · s_a[m] · s_w[n]. The QDQ graph dequantises the same product as (s_x·s_w) · C_s32 (per-tensor), or s_x[m]·s_w[n] · C_s32 (per-axis, which is what Quark emits for weights and what SmoothQuant needs for activations). Those are the same expression: our kernel's go_rows already applies Cm·as[m]·gs[n], so a Quark-quantised model maps onto it by feeding the graph's scales instead of deriving them from amax/127. Nothing about the kernel changes; what changes is where the two numbers come from.

Folding the output QuantizeLinear is the same trick one step later: give the readback the scale 1/s_y and it emits int8 directly (y_q = clamp(round(C/s_y) + zp_y)) instead of float. The intermediate float tensor then never exists.

What works today, and what does not#

  • Works: an A8W8 QDQ graph runs on our EP unchanged. onebit_ep_qdq_proof builds exactly that pattern (int8 in / int8 out, DequantizeLinear → MatMul → QuantizeLinear) with the model editor API, and our EP claims the single MatMul out of the four nodes and returns int8 outputs identical to the CPU EP's (worst |d| = 0 LSB, no saturation). The DequantizeLinear and QuantizeLinear nodes stay on the CPU EP, which is correct but means the float tensors are still materialised.
  • Not done: claiming the three-node group (DQ, MatMul, Q) as one fused node so the dequantised floats never exist, feeding int8 activations straight into the kernel's input BO (no float quantisation step), per-axis scale plumbing through gemm_f32 (it takes one amax/127 per row today), and support for the asymmetric zero points Quark can emit. An asymmetric zero point is not free: with zp_x or zp_w non-zero the product gains the correction terms -zp_x·Σ_k w_q[k][n], -zp_w·Σ_k a_q[m][k] and +K·zp_x·zp_w, so the EP claims only zp = 0 until those are folded into the kernel's epilogue.
  • Different kernels, not a configuration: A16W8 needs int16 activations, MX/BFP16 need block scales, and Int4 weight-only is the format our own forward route already stores (Q4NX), so the natural split afterwards is our Q4NX pack for weight-only and the Quark QDQ path for A8W8.

The proof is deliberately opset-21, domain-only, symmetric and per-tensor: it pins down the claim (our EP takes the MatMul inside the pattern and the arithmetic is right) without pretending the fused fast path exists yet.
